verdict.reasoning: Patient states, "It hurts when I pee," which directly indicates pain when urinating.

Duration: Patient says symptoms have been present "For six days now." Dysuria and smell: "I've got this sting when I pee and it hurts when I go to the loo. Got this very unpleasant smell that comes out."

Location and severity: Patient reports "pain in my tummy" and clarifies it is "In the middle"; when asked severity, she answers "7." Pattern: She says pain "Comes and goes," indicating intermittent pain.
Patient reports blood in urine: "Yes, but I've had spotted blood in my urine" and later reiterates "Yeah, I've had spotting in my urine."
Fever denial: When asked about temperature, patient responds, "No, not at all" and later confirms "No fever at all."
Back/loin pain denial: Doctor asks about "lower back pain" and "loin pain," and patient responds "No" and "And no loin pain as well."
Voiding ability: Doctor asks, "have you actually been able to pass water?" and the patient answers, "Yes."
Oral intake: Doctor asks, "have you been able to eat and drink?" and the transcript notes the patient replies, "Yes."
Past medical history: In response to kidney/urine infection questions, patient says, "I had IBS before."
Medication: Patient states, "I've had Mebavin"; when asked dose and frequency, she confirms taking it regularly, "Yes," three times a day, "Yes, I do," and "200 milligrams?" – "Yes."

Antibiotic plan: Doctor says, "We can treat this infection... With a course of antibiotics... It would just be for three days." The specific antibiotic is not named, matching "unspecified oral antibiotic."

Doctor recommends sachets from the chemist: "some sachets which you can get from the chemists ... which just help change the acidity of your urine." Instructions on taking them are not explicitly discussed; the phrase "as per instructions" is not in the transcript and is an inferred detail.
Allergy: When asked about allergies, patient says "Clindamycin" and doctor repeats, "You are allergic to clindavicin," indicating clindamycin allergy.
Family history: Doctor asks, "anyone in your family had any medical problems?" and patient answers, "No," indicating no significant family illnesses.
Social history: Patient says, "I live with friends" and later, "I'm a support worker."
Alcohol: Doctor asks, "So how much in an average week?" Patient replies, "One glass of wine a week."
Smoking: When asked, "Do you smoke?" the patient responds, "No."

Assessment: Doctor states, "It sounds very much like you might have an infection in your urine." This is a clinical characterization of dysuria and hematuria as a probable lower urinary tract infection; no features of complication are mentioned.

IBS status: Doctor asks about IBS, "how's that been recently? Any change in your bowel habit, any blood when you pass stool?" Patient answers "No" to change in bowel habit and "No" to weight loss, implying IBS is unchanged/stable.

Electronic prescription: Doctor says, "I can send a prescription through to your requested pharmacy" and later confirms, "the antibiotics that I'm going to prescribe will go through to that pharmacy" (Knightsbridge practice), and "It would just be for three days."
Hydration and cranberry: Doctor advises, "drink lots of water. So two and a half to three liters a day, you can get some cranberry juice and drink that as well."

Urine-alkalinising sachets: Doctor recommends "some sachets which you can get from the chemists ... which just help change the acidity of your urine. So I can put the details of that on your notes." These are over-the-counter alkalinising sachets; while exact wording "according to instructions" is not used, using as directed is standard and implied by providing details.

Thermometer and monitoring: Doctor asks if patient has a thermometer; when she says no, he advises, "It would be helpful if you could get a thermometer from the pharmacy and do check your temperature just to make sure that it isn't going up and down."

Safety-net advice: Doctor says, "If you feel like your pain is getting worse or not settling, you get lower back pain, or you're getting a high temperature, you have any problems actually passing urine, then it's very important that we speak to you again" and adds that if symptoms recur "then it's important for us to talk to you in more detail."
Continuation of Mebavin is not discussed in the plan segment. The medication is confirmed in history, but the doctor does not explicitly advise to continue it.
System review: As above, patient denies fever: "No, not at all" and "No fever at all."
System review for pain: Patient denies "lower back pain" and says "And no loin pain as well."
Menses: Doctor asks, "Do you have regular periods?" and patient replies, "Yes, I do."
Vaginal discharge: Doctor asks, "any vaginal discharge or anything like that?" and patient responds, "No, just the blood spot in my" (urine).
